2014B16.goal: Four dice are rolled; we want the probability that at least three show the same value. Split into "exactly three equal" and "all four equal".

tools.name: Casework on exactly three vs four
Counting outcomes
tools.why: Choose the repeated value, which dice show it, and the odd die's value.

2014B16.approach: Count outcomes out of $6^4=1296$. Exactly three equal: choose the value ($6$), the three dice ($4$), and a different value for the last die ($5$). All four equal: $6$.

check.q: How many ways to choose which $3$ of $4$ dice match?

2014B16.bridge: Count exactly-three and all-four outcomes and divide by $6^4$.
2014B16.shortcut: "At least $k$ the same" is always exactly-$k$ plus higher cases.
traps: Forgetting the factor $5$ (the fourth die must differ).
2014B16.recognize: "At least three the same" with dice: casework by exact counts.

2014B17.goal: We want the largest power of $2$ dividing $10^{1002}-4^{501}$. Factor out the obvious powers of $2$, then find how many $2$s are in what remains.
2014B17.approach: Pull out $2^{1002}$. Split $5^{1002}-1$ as a difference of squares and find the power of $2$ in each factor using remainders mod $8$.

check.q: What is $4^{501}$ as a power of $2$?
What is the largest power of $2$ dividing $6$?

2014B17.bridge: Factor out $2^{1002}$ and count $2$s in $5^{1002}-1$ with a difference of squares.
traps: Assuming $5^{1002}-1$ has only one factor of $2$.
2014B17.recognize: Powers of a prime dividing $a^n-b^n$: factor with differences of squares and check small moduli (or use LTE).

2014B18.goal: Eleven positive integers have mean $10$ (sum $110$), median $9$ and unique mode $8$. We maximise the largest. Make the other ten as small as the rules allow.

tools.name: Unique mode
tools.fact: 8\text{ appears more often than any other value}

2014B18.approach: Try different numbers of $8$s. More $8$s raise the small values but let other values repeat more. Compare the minimum possible sum of the first ten values in each case.

steps.title: Three 8s
steps.explain: Take $a_3=a_4=a_5=8$, $a_1=a_2=1$ (two $1$s is fine, fewer than three $8$s). Then $a_6=9$, and above the median each value may appear at most twice: $9,10,10,11$. Sum of the first ten: $1+1+8+8+8+9+9+10+10+11=75$.

check.q: With three $8$s as the mode, how many times may $10$ appear?
check.why: It must appear fewer times than $8$.

steps.title: Compare other cases
steps.explain: Two $8$s: other values appear once: $1,2,3,8,8,9,10,11,12,13$ sum $77$. Four $8$s: $1,8,8,8,8,9,9,9,10,10$ sum $80$. So three $8$s gives the smallest sum, $75$.

2014B18.bridge: Minimise the first ten values under the median and mode rules; the eleventh is $110$ minus that.
solution: With three $8$s: $1,1,8,8,8,9,9,10,10,11$ (sum $75$) respects the unique mode.
Other mode counts give larger sums ($77$, $80$).
2014B18.shortcut: Small values may repeat as long as they repeat fewer times than the mode.
traps: Forcing all small values to be distinct.
2014B18.recognize: Maximise one value under mean/median/mode constraints: minimise all others, trying each possible mode frequency.

2014B19.goal: Two random points on the outer circle (radius $2$) form a chord. We want the probability it crosses the inner circle (radius $1$). That depends only on the angle between the points.

tools.name: Distance from centre to a chord
tools.why: $\theta$ is the central angle; the perpendicular bisects it.

tools.name: Uniform angle
tools.fact: \text{the smaller central angle is uniform on }[0^\circ,180^\circ]
tools.why: Fix the first point; the second is uniform around the circle.

2014B19.approach: The chord crosses the inner circle when its distance from the centre is less than $1$: $2\cos\tfrac\theta2<1$, i.e. $\theta>120^\circ$. Then compute the probability of that angle.

check.q: For $\theta=120^\circ$ on a circle of radius $2$, how far is the chord from the centre?

steps.title: Probability
steps.explain: The smaller central angle is uniform on $[0^\circ,180^\circ]$; $P(\theta>120^\circ)=\tfrac{60}{180}=\tfrac13$.

2014B19.bridge: Turn "crosses the inner circle" into $\theta>120^\circ$ and use the uniform angle.
solution: The chord's distance from the centre is $2\cos\tfrac\theta2$.
It meets the inner circle iff $2\cos\tfrac\theta2<1$, i.e. $\theta>120^\circ$.
$\theta$ is uniform on $[0,180^\circ]$, so the probability is $\tfrac13$.
2014B19.shortcut: Fix one point; the second must land in the arc more than $120^\circ$ away on either side: $120^\circ$ of $360^\circ$.
2014B19.recognize: Random chords from random endpoints: reduce to the central angle, which is uniform.

2014B20.goal: For how many integers is $x^4-51x^2+50<0$? It is a quadratic in $x^2$ that factors.
2014B20.approach: Factor, then find integers with $x^2$ strictly between $1$ and $50$.
2014B20.bridge: Factor in $x^2$ and count integers between the roots.
2014B20.shortcut: Treat $x^4$ problems with no odd powers as quadratics in $x^2$.

2014B21.goal: Trapezoid $ABCD$ has bases $33$ and $21$ and legs $10$ and $14$, with acute angles at $A$ and $B$. We want the shorter diagonal. Find the height and the horizontal overhangs.
2014B21.approach: The overhangs $x$ (under leg $10$) and $y$ (under leg $14$) satisfy $x+y=12$ and $y^2-x^2=96$, so $y-x=8$. Then $h$ and coordinates give both diagonals.
2014B21.bridge: Find overhangs and height, then compute both diagonals.
2014B21.shortcut: $23^2+96=625$ is a perfect square, a strong hint you are on the right diagonal.
traps: Putting the leg $10$ on the wrong side.
Forgetting the angles at $A$, $B$ are acute (overhangs point outward).
2014B21.recognize: Trapezoids with known sides: drop perpendiculars; the two Pythagorean equations subtract to a linear one.

2014B22.goal: Eight semicircles (two per side, diameter $1$) line the inside of a $2\times2$ square. A circle at the centre touches all of them. We want its radius.

tools.name: Tangent circles
tools.why: Externally tangent circles touch along the line of centres.

tools.name: Distance formula
tools.why: From the square's centre to a semicircle's centre.

2014B22.approach: Put the square at $[0,2]^2$. A semicircle on the bottom side is centred at $(\tfrac12,0)$ with radius $\tfrac12$. The central circle is centred at $(1,1)$; its radius plus $\tfrac12$ equals the distance between centres.
2014B22.bridge: Set centre distance equal to the sum of radii.
solution: Semicircle centres are at $(\tfrac12,0)$ and similar points, radius $\tfrac12$.
2014B22.shortcut: All eight semicircles are equivalent by symmetry; check one.
traps: Using the distance to the square's side.
2014B22.recognize: Circles tangent to several equal circles: distance between centres equals the sum of radii.

2014B23.goal: A sphere is inscribed in a frustum whose volume is twice the sphere's. We want the ratio of the base radii $\tfrac Rr$. Tangent lengths give a neat relation between the sphere radius and $R,r$.

tools.name: Tangent lengths
tools.why: From each base circle's edge, the two tangent segments to the sphere are equal to that base's radius.

tools.name: Height of the frustum
tools.why: The height equals the sphere's diameter $2\rho$.

2014B23.approach: In the cross-section, the frustum is an isosceles trapezoid around a circle. The slant side is $R+r$ (equal tangents), and the height is $2\rho$, giving $\rho^2=Rr$. Plug into the volume condition and solve for $t=\tfrac Rr$.

check.q: What is the larger root of $t^2-3t+1=0$?

2014B23.bridge: Use equal tangents to get $\rho^2=Rr$, then the volume condition gives a quadratic in $\tfrac Rr$.
solution: Equal tangent lengths make the slant $R+r$, so $(2\rho)^2=4Rr$.
2014B23.shortcut: The relation $\rho^2=Rr$ for a sphere in a frustum is worth remembering.
traps: Using a cone volume formula instead of the frustum's.
2014B23.recognize: Spheres inscribed in frustums (or circles in trapezoids): equal tangent lengths give $\rho^2=Rr$.

2014B24.goal: Arrange $1$–$5$ in a circle (up to rotation and reflection). It is bad if some $n$ from $1$ to $15$ is not a sum of consecutive numbers. Most $n$ are automatic; only $6$ and $7$ need checking.

tools.name: Complements on a circle
tools.why: Removing a consecutive block from a circle leaves a consecutive block.

2014B24.approach: $1$–$5$ come from single numbers and $15$ from everything. By complements, $8$–$14$ come from $7$–$1$. So an arrangement is bad iff $6$ or $7$ is missing. $6$ needs an adjacent pair $\{1,5\}$ or $\{2,4\}$ or the consecutive triple $\{1,2,3\}$; $7$ needs $\{2,5\}$, $\{3,4\}$ or $\{1,2,4\}$.

steps.title: Reduce to 6 and 7
steps.explain: If $s$ is a consecutive sum, so is $15-s$. Since $1$–$5$ are present, $10$–$14$ are too; $8,9$ follow from $7,6$. So only $6$ and $7$ matter.

check.q: If an arc sums to $4$, what does the rest of the circle sum to?

steps.title: Find the bad ones
steps.explain: Checking the $12$ arrangements: $1,2,5,3,4$ has no consecutive block summing to $6$, and $1,3,2,4,5$ has none summing to $7$. Every other arrangement has both. So $2$ bad arrangements.

check.q: In the circle $1,2,5,3,4$, which adjacent pairs exist?
check.why: Neighbours around the circle; none sums to $6$.

2014B24.bridge: Use complements to reduce to sums $6$ and $7$, then check which arrangements miss them.
solution: Consecutive sums come in pairs $s$, $15-s$, so only $6$ and $7$ need checking.
Of the $12$ arrangements, $1,2,5,3,4$ misses $6$ and $1,3,2,4,5$ misses $7$.
There are $2$ bad arrangements. The answer is $\textbf{(B)}\ 2$.
2014B24.shortcut: List the ways to make $6$ and $7$ ($\{1,5\},\{2,4\},\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{2,5\},\{3,4\},\{1,2,4\}$) and look for arrangements that avoid all of one list.
traps: Checking all $15$ sums for all $12$ arrangements by brute force (slow).
2014B24.recognize: Consecutive sums on a circle: complements pair $s$ with total $-s$, halving the work.

2014B25.goal: A frog on pads $0$–$10$ jumps down with probability $\tfrac N{10}$ from pad $N$. Starting at pad $1$, we want the chance of reaching $10$ before $0$. Use the symmetry of the setup and a chain of linear equations.

tools.name: Symmetry
tools.why: Reflecting $N\to10-N$ swaps "escape" and "eaten" and keeps the jump probabilities, and pad $5$ is fixed.

2014B25.approach: Let $P_1=p$. Use the equations for $N=1,2,3,4$ to express $P_2,\ldots,P_5$ in terms of $p$. Then set $P_5=\tfrac12$.

check.q: What is $\tfrac{145}{126}-\tfrac{0.4\cdot41}{36}$ over a common denominator $630$?

2014B25.bridge: Write each $P_N$ in terms of $P_1$ and use $P_5=\tfrac12$.
2014B25.shortcut: Symmetry at the middle pad cuts the system in half.
2014B25.recognize: Random walks with absorbing ends: first-step equations, and symmetry often pins a middle value.
